name: Goita
description: Goita is a four-player Japanese partnership shedding game from Noto in which players answer an attack tile with a matching tile (or king wildcard) and then issue a new attack.
deck: 32-tile Goita set based on shogi piece types (two kings, two rooks, two bishops, four golds, four silvers, four knights, four lances, ten pawns)

history.origins: Goita is a four-player partnership game from Ushitsu, Noto, Ishikawa prefecture, Japan, where fishermen are said to have played it at least since the early 20th century. Its immediate ancestor is the game Uke-Shogi, popular in Japan in the late 19th and early 20th century.
timeline: Late 19th to early 20th century: Uke-Shogi and related matching games recorded in Japan.
Early 20th century: Goita played by fishermen in Ushitsu, Noto.
Modern era: Published editions with cards/tiles spread play beyond Ishikawa.
history.cultural: Goita is treated as a regional heritage game in Ishikawa and is often taught as a local traditional pastime.
history.evolution: Play shifted from local wooden tiles to commercially printed card versions while preserving partnership and scoring structure.

setup.players: Exactly 4 players in fixed opposite partnerships (2v2).
setup.deck: 32 tiles/cards: 2 kings, 2 rooks, 2 bishops, 4 golds, 4 silvers, 4 knights, 4 lances, 10 pawns.
setup.dealing: All 32 tiles are distributed so each player has 8. Play and deal proceed counterclockwise.
setup.equipment: Score sheet or chips for cumulative team score.

rules.objective: Empty your hand first so your team scores the value of your final attack tile and reaches game target before opponents.
rules.gameplay: Dealer leads by placing one covered tile and one face-up attack tile. On each subsequent turn, a player may pass or respond by playing a matching tile (or a king except against lance/pawn), then immediately plays a new attack tile. If three consecutive players pass, the last successful attacker leads again with a covered tile and any new attack. Players always act by either playing two tiles or passing. The deal ends when a player plays their final pair.
keyRules: Kings can substitute only against non-lance and non-pawn attacks.
Passing is always allowed, even when a legal response exists.
A king cannot be used as an attack unless the other king is already face up or both kings are in your hand.
Special pre-play pawn holdings (five or more) can trigger immediate win/redeal outcomes.

strategy.basic: Preserve kings for difficult defenses and key tempo swings after pass chains.
strategy.intermediate: Use passes to keep partnership tempo and avoid feeding opponents favorable attack values.
strategy.advanced: Track exposed piece counts and concealed lead cards to infer hidden hand structure and endgame outs.
tips: Because action is pass or two-tile play, parity of hand size and expected response windows matters.
Coordinate implicitly with partner through attack choice; you cannot communicate explicitly.

variations.name: Pawn Check Procedure
variations.description: Tables differ on exact handling of five-to-eight pawn opening reveals, including redeal versus immediate scoring options.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Pawn-check rules vary by table; overrides can be added when implementing specific house rules.

variations.name: Initial Dealer Method
variations.description: First dealer and partnerships may be determined by drawing designated high tiles or by agreed random method.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Dealer selection is procedural only; no engine constant overrides apply for this variant.

scoring.description: Winning team scores the point value of the winner's final attack tile; some finishes after triple-pass allow doubled value when final pair is equal.
scoring.winCondition: First partnership to reach 150 cumulative points wins.

synthesis.shortDescription: A four-player Japanese team game where players alternate pass or two-tile response plays, racing to empty hand while maximizing final attack value scoring.
